newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIAN INFIGHTING INTENSIFIES AS ENVOY FLIES IN.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIAN INFIGHTING INTENSIFIES AS ENVOY FLIES IN.

text.p: Political infighting in Albania intensified on Wednesday, four days before a general election that could make or break efforts to restore stability to Europe's poorest country.
The government refused to countersign a presidential decree to regulate "pyramid" investment schemes of the type whose collapse earlier this year triggered months of bloodshed.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a Socialist, said President Sali Berisha had altered several key aspects of the draft presented by Albania's multi-party interim government.
"We cannot sign the decree which (represents) a change from the original draft presented by the government. All the changes should first be approved by the government," Malaj said.
He said there was now little hope of resolving the standoff before Sunday's parliamentary polls.

Former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky was due to arrive in Albania to iron out last-minute election difficulties, in his role as envoy for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The vote is widely seen as a judgment on Berisha's five years in office and the violent upheaval in which some 1,500 people have been killed.
Some 450 observers will watch over polling stations. A 7,000-strong multinational peacekeeping force is helping to maintain order and safeguard emergency aid supplies to the former communist country.

"Mr Vranitzky's presence is an indication of the importance attached to having this election run correctly and producing a result which is legitimate and credible for Albanians," OSCE spokesman Mark Smith said.
With time fast running out, two major procedural issues remain unresolved -- polling hours, and how to decide 40 seats under proportional representation.

All parties have agreed to close polling stations by early evening, instead of 9 p.m. under the election law, to reduce the chances of violence and cheating. But Berisha says he has no authority to issue the necessary decree.
"Mr Vranitzky will certainly have something to say about the polling hours," OSCE spokesman Mark Smith said. "The OSCE favours earlier closing to make it easier for our observers."

There is no consensus on allocating the 40 proportional seats after a court threw out a proposal to give a fixed percentage to smaller parties expected to clear a two percent minimum barrier. Two-round majority races will decide 115 seats.
Berisha's job is not on the line on Sunday, but he has been waging an aggressive campaign to keep the huge majority his right-wing Democrats won in last year's election, widely criticised as unfair.
With no reliable opinion polls, the outcome is virtually impossible to forecast, but both the Democrats and the Socialists are predicting victory.

Berisha, who was campaigning in northeastern Albania, rejects the Socialists' contention that they have thrown off the legacy of their hardline Communist predecessors, and accuses them of fomenting months of violence.

The Socialists, under economist Fatos Nano, head an interim government appointed in March at the height of the rebellion when Berisha was forced to call the early election. They brand the president a dictator bent on cheating at the polls.

According to government estimates, at least $1.2 billion in savings was wiped out when five pyramid schemes, in which interest to old depositors was paid with funds from new investors, collapsed at the start of the year.
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank had urged Berisha to take swift action on the pyramid schemes as a pre-conditon for quelling unrest. REUTERS
